title: Kinpira Gobo
subtitle: braised burdock root and carrot with soy and mirin
excerpt: Kinpira gobo is a classic Japanese side dish of julienned burdock root and carrot stir-fried and braised in soy sauce, mirin, and sake until tender-crisp and deeply savoury. It keeps well and improves over a few days. Serves 4 as a side.
sourceNotes: Kinpira is a Japanese cooking technique of stir-frying and simmering root vegetables. Gobo (burdock root) kinpira is one of the most traditional and enduring Japanese side dishes.

recipe.batchNotes: Kinpira gobo keeps in the fridge for up to 5 days. Make a large batch and serve as a ready side dish throughout the week.

glossaryTerms.definition: Burdock root, a long, thin, fibrous root vegetable with an earthy, slightly bitter flavour used in Japanese cooking. It is soaked in cold water to prevent browning.
A Japanese cooking style of stir-frying root vegetables then finishing with a glaze of soy sauce, mirin, and sake until sticky and caramelised.

content.text: burdock root into a sticky, savoury side with a pleasingly chewy bite. The burdock is soaked to remove bitterness, then stir-fried with carrot until glazed and tender-crisp. Serves 4 as a side.
Burdock root darkens quickly once cut. Have a bowl of cold water ready and drop the julienned pieces in immediately. Drain and dry well before frying.
Prepare the vegetables: julienne the carrot into thin matchsticks. If using burdock root, julienne it and soak in cold water for 10 minutes, then drain and pat dry.
Mix soy sauce, mirin, sake, and sugar in a small bowl. Set aside.
Heat the sesame oil and vegetable oil in a frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the dried chilli if using and cook for 30 seconds.
Add the carrot (and burdock if using) to the pan. Stir-fry for 3 to 4 minutes until just beginning to soften at the edges.

Pour in the glaze mixture. Toss constantly over high heat for 2 to 3 minutes until the liquid has reduced and coats the vegetables in a glossy glaze. Scatter over sesame seeds and serve warm or at room temperature.

attrs.symptom: Carrots are too soft and losing their shape
attrs.cause: The vegetables were stir-fried too long before the glaze was added.
attrs.fix: Add the glaze after only 3 to 4 minutes of frying. The sauce cooks the vegetables further.

attrs.symptom: Glaze is burning before the vegetables are cooked
attrs.cause: The heat was too high once the sauce was added.
attrs.fix: Reduce heat to medium once the glaze goes in and toss frequently to prevent scorching.

attrs.cause: The soy sauce to mirin ratio is unbalanced.
attrs.fix: Add an extra teaspoon of mirin and a pinch of sugar to round out the saltiness.

content.text: Kinpira gobo is a washoku classic, part of Japan's traditional home cooking. It is one of the dishes that every Japanese home cook makes by feel. There is almost no variation: gobo, carrot, soy, mirin. The simplicity is the point. It pairs with rice, goes into bento boxes, and sits alongside grilled fish. Burdock root is not easy to find everywhere, but the carrot alone version still holds its own.
